title: Array
short: A row of numbered boxes. Jump to any box by its number.
what: An array is a row of boxes stored side by side in memory. Each box has a number called its index, starting at 0. Because the boxes sit next to each other, the computer can jump to any index in one step. In Python it is the list.
analogy: Lockers in a school hallway. To open locker 2 you walk straight to it. You never open lockers 0 and 1 first.

frames.label: nums
frames.say: nums holds 5 values. The small numbers under the boxes are the indexes: 0 for the first box, 4 for the last.

frames.label: nums
frames.say: nums[2] reads box 2 directly. The computer works out its spot in memory, so any index takes one step.

frames.label: nums
frames.say: nums.append(8) puts 8 in the next free box at the end. No other box moves, so this is fast too.

frames.label: nums
frames.say: Now insert 5 at index 1. First, boxes 1 to 5 must each slide one place right to make room.

frames.label: nums
frames.say: 5 sits at index 1, but 5 other values had to move. Inserting near the front costs O(n): more items, more moving.

frames.label: nums
frames.say: Is 4 in the list? Without its index, Python checks box after box: 7, 5, 3, 9, then 4. That search is O(n).

frames.label: nums
frames.say: nums.pop() removes the last box and hands back 8. Like append, it moves nothing else.

when: Items in order, reached by position
Look at index i and its neighbors i - 1, i + 1
Walk from both ends or with a moving window
python:
nums = [7, 3, 9, 4, 6]
print(nums[2])
nums.append(8)
nums.insert(1, 5)
print(nums)
print(4 in nums, nums.index(4))
print(nums.pop(), nums)
print(nums[-1], nums[1:3], len(nums))
cost: Add or remove at the end
Insert or remove at the front or middle
watch: Indexes start at 0, so the last one is len(nums) - 1. nums[len(nums)] raises IndexError.
insert(0, x) or pop(0) inside a loop makes it O(n^2). Use collections.deque for a queue.
b = a does not copy the list: both names see the same boxes. Use a.copy() or a[:].
